lessons.title: DHCPv6 relay lifecycle: the UDP/547 listener is the service
lessons.body_html:
A FortiGate DHCPv6 relay is an interface-scoped forwarding service. It lets clients on one IPv6 link obtain DHCPv6 configuration from a server on another link without extending the server's Layer-2 segment. The important operational distinction is that the configuration object can remain present while the relay process has lost its UDP/547 listener.

Packet and process mechanics

A DHCPv6 client normally sends from UDP/546 to the DHCPv6 service on UDP/547, commonly using the link-local multicast destination ff02::1:2. The FortiGate relay receives the client message on the configured interface, wraps it in a DHCPv6 Relay-Forward message, and forwards it to the configured server over UDP/547. The server returns a Relay-Reply; the relay removes the outer relay envelope and forwards the enclosed response to the client link. This is not DHCPv6 prefix delegation on the FortiGate WAN interface, and it is not the IPv4 DHCP smart-relay feature.

The relay is enabled under the IPv6 settings of the client-facing interface. The configured relay server address is the remote DHCPv6 server, not the interface's own address. The routing table must provide a path to that server and the return path must reach the FortiGate. Firewall policy or upstream ACLs can still prevent the forwarded exchange even when the relay process is healthy.

Configuration shape

config system interface
    edit "port5"
        config ipv6
            set dhcp6-relay-service enable
            set dhcp6-relay-type regular
            set dhcp6-relay-ip 2001:db8:d0c::a
        end
    next
end

The documented FortiOS 8.0 example uses a regular relay type and one configured IPv6 server address. Confirm the server address, interface, IPv6 route, and return route before treating a missing client lease as a relay-process defect.

What the evidence proves

diagnose sys udpsock6 should show the dhcp6r process listening on UDP/547. That proves the process has bound the socket; it does not prove a server reply is returning. A packet capture on the client-facing interface proves whether the client solicitation reaches the FortiGate. A capture on the server-facing interface proves whether the relay forwards it and whether the server responds. Use diagnose debug application dhcp6r -1 when the socket is absent or the relay process reports an error.

Recent failure pattern and recovery

Fortinet Community documented a FortiOS 7.6.7/7.6.8 defect in which DHCPv6 relay can stop after a new DHCPv6 server is configured on an interface or after reboot. The distinguishing evidence is a missing dhcp6r UDP/547 listener and the debug message dhcp6r_socket_list_add() bind(csock): Permission denied. This is materially different from a server that receives a relay packet but fails to allocate an address.

The documented workarounds are to disable and re-enable dhcp6-relay-service, or restart dhcp6r. The Community note warns that the failure can recur after another server change or reboot; the permanent fix is identified for FortiOS 7.6.10. Treat the workaround as temporary, record the triggering event, and verify the socket and packet exchange again after any configuration change or reboot.

Operational boundary

Do not infer health from the interface configuration alone. The useful proof chain is: relay enabled, IPv6 route to server, dhcp6r bound to UDP/547, relay-forward visible on the server-facing link, and relay-reply visible on the client-facing link. In HA, validate the active unit after failover; a process-level symptom can follow the unit that becomes active.

lessons.title: IPS signature metadata API: lookup, version delta, and pagination
lessons.body_html:
FortiManager 8.0 exposes a read-only API path for querying FortiGuard IPS package and signature metadata. It is useful for security operations that need to compare signature catalogs, identify what changed between package releases, or enrich a vulnerability workflow without installing a package on managed devices.

Endpoint and request model

The documented endpoint is /um/query/productapi. The API request is a FortiManager JSON-RPC get operation; the data.target value identifies the IPS metadata operation. Three useful query forms are documented: a single signature lookup by ID, all signature details for one package release, and a delta between two package releases. The query also supports offset and limit, so a large signature set can be retrieved in pages.

{
  "id": 1,
  "method": "get",
  "params": [{
    "url": "/um/query/productapi",
    "data": {
      "target": "/srvupd/detail/ips/34.089?detail=1&offset=0&limit=10"
    }
  }],
  "session": "<FortiManager-session>"
}

For one signature, the documented target uses /fgd/lookup/ency?source=ips&id=58947. For a package release, it uses a path such as /srvupd/detail/ips/34.089?detail=1&offset=0&limit=10. For a delta, it uses a pair of versions, for example /srvupd/detail/ips/34.085/34.089?detail=1&offset=0&limit=10. A later page can start at offset 20 with the same limit.

Why the delta query matters

A full catalog query answers “what exists in this package?” A delta query answers “which signature IDs changed between these two releases?” That is a different data question and can substantially reduce the amount of data an automation system must compare. The result can feed a review, reporting, or change-control pipeline; it is not itself a FortiGate policy update or signature deployment.

Evidence and failure isolation

Inspect the JSON-RPC status and the returned data for the exact target path. Keep the package version, offset, and limit with the saved response so an incomplete first page is not mistaken for the complete catalog. If a signature lookup returns no record, check the ID and source type. If a delta appears incomplete, verify the two package versions and continue paging until the result set is exhausted. Do not use the existence of a successful API session as proof that the target path was accepted.

This endpoint is a metadata query. A package download, ADOM import, policy-package install, and device firmware task are separate operations with separate task state. Keep the automation permissions and audit trail aligned with that distinction: a read-only signature inventory job should not need permission to install a package or change a managed firewall.

Operational use

For a release comparison, persist the source and target package versions, fetch the delta in pages, deduplicate signature IDs, and retain the API response with the change record. For a single-signature investigation, query the signature ID directly and preserve the returned description and metadata. When a security team asks whether a signature was added in a release, the delta endpoint is the right evidence; a screenshot of the current package version alone cannot prove the change set.

lessons.title: Playbook editor 8.0: debug a node, replay input, and restart partially
lessons.body_html:
FortiAnalyzer 8.0 changes playbook development from “run the workflow and inspect the final result” to node-level execution. The editor can run, pause, and inspect data at each task, replay a workflow with different input, and restart from a selected node. This is an authoring and debugging capability, not a new incident trigger.

Execution model

A playbook receives context from its trigger and passes data from one task to the next. A connector action consumes fields from the previous task and produces an output object for downstream tasks. The 8.0 editor exposes that boundary: run a prior task, inspect its output in the Input pane for the next task, execute the current node, and inspect the Output pane. When a downstream action receives an empty value, the first task whose output diverges is usually more informative than the final failed action.

The editor adds replay using different input data and partial execution from a chosen node. It also adds Branch, Wait Operator, Compare, and Switch control-flow operators, plus Jinja support for conditions and loops. Unconfigured or inactive connectors are grayed out when selecting an action. That visual state is a configuration signal, not an execution error.

Designing a safe test

Use a known incident or sanitized test payload. First validate the trigger fields; then execute the task that transforms or enriches them; then inspect the exact field names and value types consumed by the next connector. A Jinja condition should be tested against the actual input object, including missing or null fields. A branch that evaluates false may be correct even when the playbook itself reports success.

Partial run is especially useful when a long workflow has a deterministic upstream result and the defect is isolated to a later node. It is not automatically safe for every action. If an upstream node creates a ticket, quarantines a host, sends an email, or changes a firewall object, replaying that node can duplicate the side effect. Start from the first failing node only when its input state is valid and the skipped upstream work has already completed.

Evidence and troubleshooting

Use the per-node Input and Output panes, connector availability state, and task execution status to separate a trigger problem from an action problem. Fortinet's older Community playbook troubleshooting material also describes fazwatchd diagnostics, including diagnose debug application fazwatchd 255 and test-application commands for triggering or inspecting playbook tasks. Use commands only where supported by the deployed release and preserve the task ID with the evidence.

If a connector is grayed out, configure and authenticate it before changing the playbook graph. If a task runs but its output lacks a field, inspect the previous node's output and the connector's returned schema. If the condition is wrong, inspect the evaluated input and Jinja expression rather than adding a second trigger. If the workflow fails after a replay, check whether the earlier task was intentionally skipped and whether the downstream task expects its side effect.

Release and operational caveats

These editor capabilities are documented for FortiAnalyzer 8.0.0. The playbook's trigger, connector credentials, and task actions still need to be valid in the target ADOM. Debugging a node does not prove that the same connector is configured in every ADOM or that a production trigger will supply identical data. Keep test inputs representative and avoid exposing credentials or personal data in saved execution samples.

lessons.title: Link monitor: multi-server probes and static-route control
lessons.body_html:
FortiSwitch link monitor is a switch-local health probe. It periodically tests one or more remote servers over IPv4 or IPv6 and can update static routes when the monitored path fails or recovers. It is not the same mechanism as FortiGate SD-WAN Performance SLA: the switch feature is tied to its own source interface, probe timers, and static-route table.

Probe mechanics and release changes

The monitor sends periodic ping or ARP probes from a selected source interface. FortiSwitchOS 7.4.3 added multiple server targets to one probe. FortiSwitchOS 7.4.2 changed the configuration model: a server address became required, IPv4 ping became the default instead of ARP, and an older gateway address was moved into the server field during upgrade. The gateway address is no longer mandatory, but the gateway and interface are still needed for static-route modification. If the server and interface are set without an explicit gateway, FortiSwitch attempts to derive it from the static routing table.

config system link-monitor
    edit "uplink-watch"
        set addr-mode ipv4
        set srcintf "port1"
        set server 198.51.100.10, 198.51.100.11
        set protocol ping
        set gateway-ip 198.51.100.1
        set interval 5
        set timeout 1
        set failtime 5
        set recoverytime 5
        set update-static-route enable
    next
end

The values above illustrate the documented CLI fields; use real probe targets and the actual next hop in production. Interval and timeout define how often a probe is sent and how long a reply can take. Failtime is the number of failed attempts before the server is declared down; recoverytime is the number of successful attempts before it is declared up.

The static-route dependency

The key caveat is explicit in the FortiSwitch guide: link monitor updates static routes only when the route under config router static includes set device. A probe can show a down server while the route remains installed if the route is not bound to the expected device. The feature is supported only in the default VRF instance, so placing the probe in a non-default VRF is not a valid way to isolate a tenant's route table.

config router static
    edit 10
        set dst 203.0.113.0 255.255.255.0
        set gateway 198.51.100.1
        set device "port1"
    next
end

Verification and troubleshooting

get system link-monitor shows the configured probe. diagnose sys link-monitor status all shows current probe status. Read those results alongside the static route configuration, source interface, gateway, address mode, protocol, and VRF. If the probe is down but the route remains, check the route's set device field before increasing failtime. If an upgrade changes probe behavior, verify that the server and protocol migrated as expected; do not assume the old gateway field still means the same thing.

Multiple targets help reduce dependence on one remote peer, but the targets should represent the actual path whose reachability matters. A probe to a public resolver does not prove that a private MPLS destination is reachable. Choose ping when IP reachability is the objective and ARP when the monitored target is on the local Layer-2 segment. The evidence must match the failure domain you intend to withdraw.

lessons.title: Per-radio VAP capacity: eight by default, sixteen on selected models
lessons.body_html:
A Virtual Access Point (VAP) is the radio-facing instance of an SSID and its associated wireless configuration. FortiAP 8.0 keeps eight VAPs per radio as the default, but selected G- and K-series models can support up to sixteen. The increase is a model capability and a controller/profile setting; it is not a universal limit change for every FortiAP.

Configuration layers

The global wireless-controller setting defines the maximum number of SSIDs that a radio can support. The WTP profile then assigns VAPs to a particular radio. The AP model determines whether the requested limit is supported. All three layers must agree: setting the global ceiling to sixteen does not make an older radio capable of advertising sixteen VAPs, and creating sixteen VAP objects does not mean all are assigned to the same radio.

config wireless-controller global
    set max-vap-per-radio 16
end

After setting the ceiling, edit the relevant WTP profile and add the intended VAPs to the radio. Fortinet documents that the default is eight and that selected G/K models support a choice of eight or sixteen. Keep the number of VAPs as low as practical: each additional SSID adds beacon/probe overhead, expands policy and authentication combinations, and increases the amount of wireless configuration that must be maintained.

Why an eighth SSID can fail

A Community troubleshooting tip describes a profile that rejects an eighth SSID with an “at most 7 VAPs can be configured” message. That symptom should not lead directly to disabling roaming or background scanning. First identify the exact AP model and radio, inspect the global VAP ceiling, and check the WTP profile. On older platforms, scanning and radio features can affect the effective capacity. The sixteen-VAP capability is documented only for selected G/K models; it should not be projected onto every radio or every firmware build.

Evidence and isolation

Use show wireless-controller global to confirm max-vap-per-radio. Inspect the WTP profile to see which VAPs are assigned to each radio, then compare that list with the AP model's supported limit. Check the AP's actual radio state and advertised SSIDs; the number of VAP objects in the controller database does not prove that each is being broadcast. If the profile is accepted but a client cannot see an SSID, move from capacity validation to radio/VAP status and beacon evidence.

Design implications

Use separate WTP profiles where model families have different radio capabilities. Avoid adding a VAP simply because the controller allows it; map each SSID to a real segmentation or service requirement. When a seven- or eight-VAP limit appears, distinguish a global configuration ceiling from a hardware or scanning-resource limit. The operational goal is predictable airtime and policy behavior, not the maximum possible SSID count.

lessons.title: IPv6 support boundary: endpoint access is not IPv6 device discovery
lessons.body_html:
FortiNAC 9.4 supports IPv6 for endpoint Portal and Agent communication and for administrator access to the UI. That does not mean the Inventory subsystem can discover and manage network devices using IPv6-only management addresses. Fortinet documents a clear boundary between the endpoint-facing plane and network-device management.

What is supported

Both eth1 and eth0 support IPv4 and IPv6. IPv6 endstations can communicate with the FortiNAC Portal and Agents through the endpoint-facing service. The admin UI can be accessed through the IPv6 address assigned to eth0. When a host or device uses IPv6, its IPv6 address appears in Host View or Adapter View alongside any IPv4 addresses associated with it. FortiNAC can also poll L3 IP-to-MAC information for IPv6 addresses from the documented vendor set: Cisco, Juniper EX, HP ProCurve, Brocade, and FortiGate.

What is not supported

Network-device management and Inventory discovery still require the networking equipment to have an IPv4 address. The documentation lists creation/discovery of network devices in Inventory as not supported for IPv6. This means a dual-stack endpoint can reach the portal over IPv6 while a switch with only an IPv6 management address remains undiscoverable. It is not contradictory; the two flows use different interfaces and different management protocols.

Operational flow and evidence

Separate the paths when testing. Verify that an IPv6 host can reach the Portal/Agent service on the endpoint-facing interface. Verify that an administrator can reach the UI using the IPv6 address on eth0. Then inspect the managed switch/router's management address and Inventory discovery status. If the device has no IPv4 management address, the documented limitation is the first explanation to test. If it does have IPv4, investigate the normal SNMP/CLI reachability and credential path.

For L3 polling, do not assume that every network-device vendor returns IPv6 IP-to-MAC information. Fortinet lists specific supported platforms and instructs customers to contact Support for additional device support. An IPv6 address displayed in Host View proves that FortiNAC has learned or associated that host address; it does not prove that every switch's IPv6 neighbor table is being polled.

Design and troubleshooting

Use IPv6 for the endpoint, Portal, Agent, and admin access paths where required, but retain IPv4 management reachability for network-device discovery. Document the distinction in dual-stack designs so that a failed Inventory add is not misdiagnosed as an endpoint IPv6 problem. If the portal works and the switch does not appear, check the switch management address and vendor support before changing the portal or agent configuration.

lessons.title: Native Entra ID authentication for 802.1X: the supplicant method is part of the design
lessons.body_html:
FortiNAC-F 7.6.3 adds Microsoft Entra ID as a native authentication source for username/password or certificate authentication in RADIUS 802.1X and portal login. This is not the same flow as browser-based SAML SSO. For wired or wireless 802.1X, the endpoint supplicant, access device, FortiNAC-F RADIUS virtual server, service connector, and Entra ID must agree on the authentication method.

RADIUS transaction

The endpoint supplicant starts EAP with the switch or AP. The network device acts as the RADIUS client and sends the request to the FortiNAC-F virtual server. FortiNAC-F selects the configured authentication source and EAP method, then uses the Entra ID service connector and domain mapping to validate the identity. The result returns as Access-Accept or Access-Reject; network access policy is a subsequent decision. A successful credential test against a firewall is not proof that the actual 802.1X exchange uses the same EAP method or identity format.

Configuration sequence

Create the Microsoft Entra ID service connector under Network > Service Connectors. Create the domain mapping and select that connector. Open Network > RADIUS > Virtual Servers, edit the intended virtual server, enable the supported EAP types, and set the Authentication Source to the Entra ID connector. Configure the endpoint supplicant to use the matching method. Fortinet's 7.6.5 cookbook documents TTLS-PAP for username/password authentication, a certificate-based path, and captive-portal authentication. The 7.6.3 release notes establish the native Entra ID feature; use the guide for the exact workflow supported by the deployed build.

Community failure pattern

A Community thread about hybrid Entra ID users describes a useful diagnostic boundary: fully cloud-based users authenticate, while hybrid users receive RADIUS Access-Reject even though a basic FortiGate credential test succeeds. The reply identifies a Windows supplicant mismatch: the client may default to PEAP, while the documented Entra ID 802.1X flow expects TTLS. The endpoint can therefore reject the exchange before the identity provider is the real problem.

Evidence and remediation

Capture the actual RADIUS Access-Request/Access-Reject and inspect the FortiNAC-F RADIUS logs. Verify the virtual server's supported EAP methods, authentication source, service connector status, domain mapping, and Windows supplicant profile. Test with the exact endpoint method rather than relying on a simple username/password check. If certificate authentication is used, validate the required TLS service configuration and certificate chain. For TEAP, primary and secondary authentication order is significant; do not reuse a TEAP profile for a TTLS-PAP test.

Boundary

Keep the RADIUS 802.1X flow separate from SAML portal SSO. SAML redirect success proves browser federation; it does not prove EAP negotiation, RADIUS policy selection, or supplicant compatibility. Conversely, a working TTLS-PAP test does not prove that the portal's SAML connector is correct.

lessons.title: TACACS+/RADIUS client groups: policy scope at scale
lessons.body_html:
FortiAuthenticator 8.0.2 adds client-group objects for TACACS+ and RADIUS. A client group is a reusable set of network access servers (NAS devices) that can be selected by a policy. It is not a user group, an identity source, or a command-authorization profile. Its purpose is to make policy scope manageable when hundreds of switches, routers, and other clients are configured.

Object relationships

Each NAS client still needs its own address or subnet definition and shared secret. The administrator groups those client objects and selects one or more groups when creating a TACACS+ policy. The policy can combine individual clients and client groups. When a NAS sends a request, FortiAuthenticator identifies the client by its source address and uses the configured client/group scope to determine which policy can apply. The identity source and authorization behavior are configured in the policy; the group only defines which clients are in scope.

The new TACACS+ API endpoints are /tacplusclientgroups/ for group objects, /tacplusgroupclient/ for group/client associations, and /tacpluspolicygroup/ for policy/group associations. This makes group membership and policy binding automatable without turning every policy into a long list of individual NAS entries.

Configuration sequence

Under Authentication > TACACS+ Service > Clients, create or import the individual clients, then use the Group tab to create a group and move the intended clients into the chosen list. Under Authentication > TACACS+ Service > Policies, select the group in the TACACS+ client groups field. FortiAuthenticator 8.0.2 also documents client groups for RADIUS. Keep address scopes precise: a broad subnet group can unintentionally include devices that should use a different policy.

Verification

Check the group membership table, then inspect the policy's chosen client groups. Use the API to read back the group and association objects after automation. Finally, test a request from a NAS in the group and another NAS outside it. Authentication logs should identify the requesting client and the selected policy. A successful API create response proves that an object was created; it does not prove that the new client was added to the group or that the policy references the group.

Common failure

A new switch is added as a TACACS+ client, but the intended policy does not match. The likely fault is not command authorization; it is an incomplete client-group association or a policy that still references only individual clients. Confirm the client address, shared secret, group membership, and policy scope before changing the identity source. If several groups overlap, simplify the address design so that a NAS does not match ambiguous client definitions.

Scale and security caveat

Client groups reduce policy administration, but they also create another object relationship to maintain. Treat a group change as an access-control change: review which NAS devices will inherit the policy, log the API response, and perform a read-after-write check. The feature changes policy scope, not the strength of the TACACS+ authentication or the command authorization rules themselves.

lessons.title: RADIUS Message-Authenticator: protect packet integrity without weakening compatibility defaults
lessons.body_html:
FortiPAM 1.9.0 adds Message-Authenticator support to its RADIUS requests and a control that determines whether the attribute is required in the RADIUS response. The attribute is a packet-integrity check defined for RADIUS extensions; it is not the same as RadSec, which transports RADIUS inside TLS.

What changes on the wire

FortiPAM sends an Access-Request with the Message-Authenticator attribute (attribute 80). The RADIUS server processes the request and returns Access-Accept or Access-Reject. When require-message-authenticator is enabled, FortiPAM expects the response to contain the attribute and validates it. The option is enabled by default in FortiPAM 1.9.0. This strengthens the exchange against forged or modified packets and aligns with mitigations introduced after the Blast-RADIUS vulnerability.

config user radius
    edit "FAC-RADIUS"
        set require-message-authenticator enable
    next
end

The option controls response validation. It does not configure the remote server to generate the attribute. If the RADIUS server is old or configured not to return Message-Authenticator, the connectivity test can fail even though the shared secret, route, and UDP reachability are correct.

Evidence

Use a packet capture to inspect whether attribute 80 is present in the Access-Request and response. RADIUS server debug may report that a packet does not contain the required Message-Authenticator attribute. Check the FortiPAM RADIUS server object and confirm the effective require-message-authenticator state. A successful ping to the RADIUS server proves only IP reachability; it does not prove that the RADIUS message meets the integrity requirement.

Compatibility decision

The preferred remediation is to update the RADIUS server so that it returns Message-Authenticator and keep FortiPAM validation enabled. FortiPAM documents disabling the option as a compatibility workaround when the server does not provide the attribute. That should be an explicit, reviewed exception, not the default response to every failed test. If the remote service is FortiAuthenticator, do not confuse FortiPAM's per-server control with FortiAuthenticator's global client-side requirement; changing a global FAC setting can weaken validation for other RADIUS clients.

Troubleshooting sequence

First confirm the request leaves FortiPAM and reaches the intended server. Next inspect the server's response and attribute 80. If the server rejects the request before a response, inspect its policy and client definition. If the server returns Access-Accept without Message-Authenticator, the FortiPAM response-validation setting explains the failure. After any compatibility change, repeat the packet capture and document the security trade-off.

A Community article describes the earlier interoperability problem in which FortiPAM connectivity to FortiAuthenticator failed because the server required Message-Authenticator while the client did not send it. FortiPAM 1.9 changes that client behavior. Use the current release documentation rather than carrying forward an old global workaround.

lessons.title: Report design templates: report, folder, and root precedence
lessons.body_html:
FortiSIEM 7.5.1 separates report data from the PDF layout used to present it. A Report Design Template controls the cover page, table of contents, sections, text, images, charts, and report tables. The template can be assigned at report, folder, or report-bundle scope. The renderer resolves a template using a documented precedence order, which explains why the same report can export with a different layout when opened from another folder.

Template resolution

For a report under Resources > Reports, FortiSIEM chooses a report-specific template first. If none exists, it uses the template assigned to the folder that currently contains the report. If neither exists, it falls back to the system-defined template for the root Reports folder. System-defined templates cannot be edited. If the same report appears in two folders and each folder has a template, the template for the folder currently being viewed is used. For Service Provider deployments, templates are defined at Super/Global and apply to customers.

Where templates are created

The Reports table includes a Report Design Template column showing the template selected for each report. A template can be created for an individual report, a report folder, or a Report Bundle. The designer provides organization and orientation controls, a cover page, table of contents, pages/sections, and objects such as text, images, charts, and report tables. Preview shows the generated PDF layout before it is saved. Restore to Default removes custom templates and leaves the default templates available.

When exporting from Analytics, the Defined option uses the normal template-resolution rules. The New option creates a one-off format for that report instance. That distinction matters when a user says that an export “ignored” a saved template: the export may have been generated with New rather than Defined.

Evidence and troubleshooting

Start with the Report Design Template column on the exact report row. If the layout is unexpected, identify the report's current folder context and check whether a report-specific template exists. Do not assume a folder template overrides a report-specific template; it is the fallback. If the template is global, verify the organization and whether the user is logged in as Super/Global. A template visible in one organization is not automatically available to another scope.

For a report that is stored in multiple folders, open it from the folder whose layout is expected and preview the export. For a bundle, inspect the bundle template rather than editing one of the member reports and assuming that the bundle will inherit it. The template name encodes organization and scope, which helps identify an unexpected assignment.

Operational caveats

Template changes affect presentation, not the underlying event query or report dataset. If a chart is missing data, investigate the report query and time range separately from the PDF template. Conversely, if the data is correct but the cover page or section layout is wrong, changing the dataset will not fix it. Keep report design and data selection as separate troubleshooting planes.

lessons.title: BGP MED in multi-hub Secure Private Access
lessons.body_html:
FortiSASE 26.1.107 adds two BGP MED controls for deployments where multiple Secure Private Access (SPA) hubs advertise the same prefix. The feature addresses a specific BGP path-selection boundary: by default, MED is generally compared only between routes learned from the same neighboring autonomous system. If two SPA hubs are in different ASNs, the preferred MED may not participate in the comparison.

Two controls, two effects

Always Compare MED forces FortiSASE to evaluate MED values for routes received from different ASNs. This makes MED a consistent decision input regardless of the neighboring AS origin. Deterministic MED groups routes by neighboring AS before comparing MED, making the comparison more predictable when several routes for the same prefix arrive from different peers. They are related but not interchangeable: one changes whether cross-AS MED is considered; the other standardizes how routes are grouped for comparison.

When it matters

Assume SPA Hub A and SPA Hub B advertise the same destination prefix, but the hubs use different ASNs. Hub A advertises a lower MED because it has the preferred path to the destination. With default behavior, FortiSASE may ignore the MED difference across ASNs and choose a path based on other BGP attributes. Enabling Always Compare MED makes the MED values participate in that cross-AS decision. Deterministic MED reduces inconsistent outcomes when routes from multiple neighboring AS groups are compared.

Configuration and availability

The controls are under Network > BGP > Advanced BGP settings > BGP MED Settings. In 26.1.107 the settings are a select-availability feature and are not visible in the portal by default. FortiCare must enable the feature for a new or existing instance through a support request. A missing setting is therefore not proof that the instance is on the wrong release; check feature enablement with Support.

Verification

Use a controlled test in which at least two SPA hubs advertise the same prefix from different ASNs with deliberately different MED values. Compare the received routes, neighboring AS, MED, and selected best path before and after enablement. If the routes have different prefixes, MED comparison is not the reason one route wins. If local preference or another higher-precedence BGP attribute differs, changing MED may not change the best path.

Design caveats

MED is a path-selection hint, not a substitute for local preference or a complete traffic-engineering design. Align MED intent across hubs and confirm that the advertisements are for the same prefix. Treat the feature as a control-plane change: record the current path, enable the requested option through FortiCare, and validate route convergence at the Security PoP before relying on it for production failover.

lessons.title: Overlay-as-a-Service: FGFM transport and transactional apply/rollback
lessons.body_html:
FortiCloud Overlay-as-a-Service (OaaS) is a cloud-orchestrated SD-WAN overlay workflow. The FortiGate spoke has an OaaS agent that communicates with the FortiCloud controller through the FGFM management tunnel. The agent validates and compares the orchestrated FortiOS configuration, applies it as a transaction, and rolls back all orchestrated changes if any configuration change fails.

Control-plane mechanics

The OaaS portal creates a target configuration for the site. The FortiCloud controller sends the orchestration through the FGFM management tunnel to the spoke. The local agent compares the target with the current FortiOS configuration, validates the changes, and applies them transactionally. A successful operation advances the configuration version and reports sync success. If a change cannot be applied, the agent rolls back the orchestrated changes rather than leaving a partial configuration that might interrupt spoke traffic.

Each FortiGate used by the FortiCloud OaaS portal must have the SD-WAN Overlay as a Service license. Check System > FortiGuard > License Information. The CLI status command is get oaas status; it reports account/site information, configuration version, sync status, target version, task ID, and error text.

Verifying a task

get oaas status
show system sdwan

Use the task ID and target version to correlate the portal task with the spoke. If the portal reports a failed task, inspect the target path and error detail before changing the SD-WAN configuration manually. A successful FGFM tunnel proves that the management path exists; it does not prove that the target SD-WAN objects can be applied.

Community failure pattern

A Fortinet Community troubleshooting tip documents a portal task that failed with “Failed to delete the zone of your device” and a target path under system/sdwan/service. The OaaS default service rule uses ID 1. If an existing service rule occupies that ID, the orchestration can fail while attempting to manage the default zone/service. The documented remedy is to duplicate the existing service rule with a different ID and remove the conflicting ID 1 rule before retrying the portal task.

Inspect show system sdwan and the service entries rather than changing unrelated ISP costs or deleting a zone blindly. The status output should be checked after the change to confirm that the task has synchronized and the configuration version advanced.

Distinction from on-box overlay orchestration

This lesson is not the same as Fabric Overlay Orchestrator with IPAM. That feature creates overlay addressing and routing on-box. OaaS is about the FortiCloud controller-to-agent transaction, FGFM management transport, configuration validation, and rollback behavior. Both can participate in SD-WAN overlay designs, but their control planes and failure evidence differ.

Operational caveats

Keep the OaaS license current on every participating FortiGate, preserve the portal task ID, and verify the spoke status after any failed task. Do not assume a failed portal task left no change until the rollback and current configuration are checked. Conversely, do not hand-edit the spoke to “fix” a portal task until the target configuration and reserved object IDs are understood.
